title: Senior's toolkit: keys, signatures and TLS
summary: Generate and inspect key pairs, sign and verify from the shell and in .NET, and see what a TLS server really sends.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: keys, signatures and TLS
steps.body: Public-key crypto at work means making key pairs, checking signatures between two systems and debugging TLS connections. These are the commands and APIs for each.

toolkit.what: Generate a private key (PEM, PKCS#8) for any algorithm.
flags: a P-256 key for ECDSA or ECDH

toolkit.what: Read a key: extract the public half to share, or print what is inside.
flags: print the key's components instead of the key
the input is a public key

toolkit.what: Sign a file with an EC or RSA key, or verify a signature. Prints `Verified OK` on success. Its ECDSA signatures are DER-encoded.
toolkit.example:
openssl dgst -sha256 -sign signing-key.pem -out release.sig release.zip
openssl dgst -sha256 -verify signing-pub.pem -signature release.sig release.zip

toolkit.what: Make the SSH key you use for Git hosts and servers, and print key fingerprints to compare with what a server shows.
flags: the key type to use today
a comment that says whose key it is
show the fingerprint of an existing key

toolkit.what: Open a TLS connection and print the handshake: protocol, cipher, and the certificate chain the server really sends.
flags: send SNI, so a shared server picks the right certificate
print every certificate in the chain, not just the leaf
close stdin so it exits after the handshake

toolkit.what: Read a certificate: who it is for, who issued it, when it expires, which names it covers.
flags: the certificate's owner and its issuer
the host names it is valid for
the fingerprint to pin or compare
toolkit.example: openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -dates -ext subjectAltName

toolkit.what: .NET signing with ECDSA. Keys move between systems as PEM. .NET's default signature format is the 64-byte IEEE P1363 form, not DER.
flags: verify a DER signature from OpenSSL, Java or Go
read a PEM key / write the public key as PEM

toolkit.what: RSA in .NET. Always name the padding: OAEP with SHA-256 to encrypt, PSS to sign. PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption is the legacy padding that allows oracle attacks.
flags: encrypt a small secret such as a DEK
toolkit.example:
using var rsa = RSA.Create(3072);
byte[] wrapped = rsa.Encrypt(dek, RSAEncryptionPadding.OaepSHA256);

steps.explain: A P-256 signature in .NET's default format is two 32-byte numbers side by side. ECDSA signatures are randomised, so the bytes change every run, but the length and the verify results do not. Change one character and verification fails.

steps.prompt: A Go service signs messages with ECDSA P-256. Your .NET code imports its public key from PEM and calls `ec.VerifyData(data, sig, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256)`. It always returns `False`, and the signatures are 70 to 72 bytes long. Why?
options: The signatures are DER-encoded; pass `DSASignatureFormat.Rfc3279DerSequence` to `VerifyData`
Go uses a different P-256 curve from .NET
The PEM import silently failed, so the key is random
ECDSA cannot be verified on a different platform from the one that signed
steps.explain: OpenSSL, Go and Java write ECDSA signatures as a DER sequence (about 70-72 bytes for P-256). .NET defaults to the fixed 64-byte P1363 form. The length is the clue: same key, same math, different envelope.

steps.prompt: `curl https://billing.internal` fails with `SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate`, but it works in the browser. `openssl s_client -connect billing.internal:443 -servername billing.internal -showcerts` shows one certificate and `verify error:num=20`. What is the likely fix?
options: Configure the server to send its intermediate certificate with the leaf (the full chain)
Renew the certificate; it has expired
steps.explain: Browsers often fetch or cache missing intermediates; curl and most HTTP clients do not. `-showcerts` printing only the leaf confirms the server sends an incomplete chain. `-k` turns verification off, which defeats TLS.

steps.prompt: See every certificate the server sends for `api.example.com`, the right one on a shared IP.
steps.explain: `-servername` sends SNI, without which a shared server may hand you its default certificate. `-showcerts` prints the whole chain.

steps.prompt: Which command do you reach for?
items: See which certificate a server really presents
Check that SNI picks the right certificate on a shared host
Find out when a certificate file expires
List the host names a downloaded certificate covers
Create a P-256 private key for signing releases
Create the key you add to your GitHub account

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When two systems disagree about a signature, compare formats before keys: PEM or DER, P1363 or DER signature, which padding. When a TLS call fails, run `openssl s_client -servername -showcerts` first and read the chain; it answers most certificate tickets in a minute.
